summary: Provincetown's Long Point Light at the tip of Cape Cod: first lit 1827, its 1875 brick tower, a 1898 gale, the 1933 bell struck by hand, and automation in 1952.

lens.where: Fourth-order Fresnel by 1926 (NRHP) and until a modern optic replaced it at automation in 1952 (LighthouseFriends); the current optic is a solar LED (USLHS)

structures.note: Square brick tower, 38 ft (NRHP). The USLHS record gives 36 ft from base to lantern.
Wood-frame keeper's house on pilings (LighthouseFriends). NRHP says the former dwelling was retained in 1875; LighthouseFriends says it was removed long ago.
Probably built with the tower (NRHP); LighthouseFriends dates it to 1904; USLHS lists 1870s.
Fog-bell tower with a 1,200-pound bell; the fog-station building was removed (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Grounds open and tower closed (LighthouseFriends). The USLHS record says not open to the public. Reached by a 2.7-mile walk from Provincetown, by shuttle, or by kayak.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1826 (Rowlett's directory) differs from USLHS (established 1827), NRHP (first illuminated 1827) and LighthouseFriends (in service the year after the 1826 Act). The story gives 1827.
LighthouseFriends: fifth-order Fresnel in 1856; USLHS: sixth-order Fresnel in 1856. Not resolved; both reported.
NRHP: probably built with the tower (1875); LighthouseFriends: dates from 1904; USLHS: 1870s. Not resolved.
NRHP says the former keeper's dwelling was retained in 1875; LighthouseFriends describes a new frame dwelling in the 1874-75 campaign and later says the dwelling was removed. Not resolved.
LighthouseFriends gives 1981 for the solar panels; the nomination gives 1982.
USLHS: not open to the public. LighthouseFriends: grounds open, tower closed. The story gives LighthouseFriends' description and the USLHS flag.
Roster and LighthouseFriends: Theodore L. Chase; the 1933 Bulletin: Thomas L. Chase. The story reports both.

notes_for_editor: Roster matched by name; the USLHS place sits 1.8 km from the station record (USLHS positions are only to the minute), so check the match. Most of the narrative rests on LighthouseFriends, which quotes the Boston Daily Globe of 1899 (Portland Gale, wife at the bell) and an 1838 Carpender report; neither was read directly. One Chronicling America search for the 1898-99 keeper and gale (Samuel S. Smith, Long Point, Massachusetts) returned no pages. Leads not used: the 1902 Life-Saving Service annual report describes a stranding on 'Long Point Reef' in September 1901 whose surfmen took off the crew; the station is not named in the text read, so it is not tied to this light. Do not confuse this station with other Long Points: the 1920 Bulletin's dwelling move was at Long Point, North Carolina; the 1924 Bulletin's lightning fire at Long Point Light was in Louisiana; the 1893-94 Board reports' Long Point beacon No. 8 is in North Carolina; the 1894 Board's fog-signal test lay off Long Point while testing the Race Point whistle. Access: LighthouseFriends says grounds open and tower closed; the USLHS record says not open to the public. Check before any visitor guidance is published. Fact-check 2026-10-22: the Chase bell is 'thousand-pound' in the 1933 Bulletin (PDF page 15) but 1,200 pounds for the 1875 bell in LighthouseFriends; not reconciled. The 1900 repairs list (scan page 60) gives no reason for Long Point's entry. The roster has 22 stints for 20 men (Derby and Samuel S. Smith each have two).
